# Danish Animal Production Benchmark for Circular Nordic Food Systems

## Dataset boundary and method

This is a **benchmark-only** dataset, not a policy narrative and not a Norway pilot case. I have prioritised Danish primary sources and close-to-primary sector sources: Danmarks Statistik and StatBank table identifiers, Danish law and executive orders on Retsinformation, government agreement texts, Folketinget committee materials for bill status, Energistyrelsen, Mejeriforeningen, and Arla’s own policy and annual reporting. Where a figure could not be recovered from a reviewed primary source in a methodologically clean way, I leave the cell blank and label that explicitly as **not found** or **needs-data** rather than backfilling with media estimates. citeturn11search1turn25search1turn29search0turn36search1

For tables below, the **URL** column uses a clickable citation plus the official table/report handle, rather than printing raw long URLs. That keeps the dataset auditable while staying within this interface. Where I calculate a value from official quarterly series, I label it as **inferens** and state the method. No years or geographies are mixed within a row.

**Status map used in this report**

| label | meaning |
|---|---|
| benchmark-only | sufficiently grounded for benchmarking use |
| needs-primary-check | source exists, but current legal or quantitative status should be re-checked before policy use |
| needs-data | reviewed sources did not yield a clean benchmark figure |
| watchlist | active policy pipeline or rapidly changing area |

## Scale of Danish swine and dairy

The cleanest current livestock stock figures are the latest point-in-time inventories: **12.3 million pigs on 1 January 2026** and **548,000 dairy cows on 31 December 2025**. For annual output, Danmarks Statistik’s quarterly release allows a full-year calculation for milk in **2025**, while the most directly retrievable pork tonnage in the reviewed material is the annual DST series for **2024** and quarterly pig-flow data for **2025**. This means the benchmark is slightly asymmetric: current inventories are newer than the clean annual pork tonnage source I could recover. citeturn39view2turn39view0turn39view1turn41search4turn41search3

## Nitrogen, land regulation and the Green Tripartite policy stack

The core **adopted** Danish nitrogen regime is still the existing **gødskningsloven** and its annual executive orders, not the full Green Tripartite replacement model. The current law’s purpose is to regulate fertiliser use so as to limit nitrogen leaching, and the 2025/26 fertiliser order sets crop-specific N and P norms for the plan period. The reviewed official material also states that Denmark applies its nitrates action programme on its whole territory and regulates manure storage, application windows and the amounts of manure and mineral fertiliser applied through the livestock and fertiliser law package. citeturn25search1turn20search4turn22view4turn46search8turn46search9

For manure intensity, the official guidance and executive-order chain still anchor the general ceiling at **170 kg N/ha from organic fertiliser**, with a derogation path for qualifying cattle farms up to **230 kg N/ha**. That is not new Green Tripartite law; it is part of the standing nitrates/derogation framework. citeturn27search0turn27search3turn28search1turn28search0

The **Green Tripartite** itself is presently a layered package: first a June 2024 political framework agreement; then a November 2024 political implementation agreement; then specific sub-agreements and draft legislation. The implementation agreement explicitly says the parties commit to vote for the legislation needed to implement the package, which means the agreement itself is not the same thing as enacted law. Folketinget materials from October 2025 and February 2026 still refer to the key nutrient and greenhouse-gas bill as a **draft law / planned law**. citeturn14search16turn22view1turn17search2turn22view2turn17search6

The agreement text is nevertheless concrete on direction and target architecture. It provides for a land-conversion package centred on **250,000 hectares of new forest by 2045** and **140,000 hectares of carbon-rich lowland soils including edge areas by 2030**; it also says the current mark regulation in 2027 is to be replaced by a new emissions-based nitrogen regulation model, and that in acute areas the tightened environmental guarantee can be set at a level where field regulation would in practice lead to fallowing. That is politically agreed text, but not itself proof that those elements are already enacted in statute today. citeturn23view0turn23view1turn24view0turn24view3

On the agricultural greenhouse-gas tax, the June 2024 agreement states that a **CO2e tax on livestock emissions** is to start in **2030**, with an effective rate of **DKK 120/t CO2e in 2030** rising to **DKK 300/t CO2e in 2035** after a 60% basic deduction, and a 2032 review. The same agreement says legislation still needs to be prepared because the tax requires data and system infrastructure. A separate expert-committee publication in 2025 summarises the agreement as one under which agricultural climate charges are to take effect from **2028 and 2030** for different sources, but that is interpretive context around the agreement, not the enacted legal text itself. I did **not** find a reviewed Retsinformation law showing that a general livestock CO2e tax is already in force in June 2026. citeturn23view5turn23view6turn23view7turn23view4turn30search4turn22view1

## What is actually documented on any swine downscaling

The official evidence base does **not** support a simple claim that Denmark is already in a regulatorily enforced national pig-herd downscaling phase. The most recent pig inventory in the reviewed official material shows **12.3 million pigs on 1 January 2026**, up **6.0%** from 1 January 2025, and the fourth quarter of 2025 saw **4.2 million pigs slaughtered**, up **16%** year on year from fourth quarter 2024. Those facts do not look like a current national forced contraction. citeturn39view2turn39view0turn41search9

At the same time, the historical series show that earlier years did experience contraction. The DST annual series embedded in the reviewed releases show **pigmeat production of 466.1 million kg in 2022**, down **10.2%** year on year, and **464.1 million kg in 2024**, down **5.2%** year on year. So the primary-source story is not “no contraction ever”; it is “contraction has occurred in specific years, but I did not find reviewed primary evidence of a current, enacted, economy-wide pig-reduction mandate”. citeturn42view1turn41search5

The Green Tripartite documents do show instruments that could indirectly constrain livestock-intensive farming in some catchments: stronger land conversion, acute-area packages, temporary higher regulation, targeted state purchases, and, if necessary, expropriation for land measures in specific water catchments. But that is still different from an enacted national pig-cap or a nationwide pig-herd reduction order. citeturn24view3turn22view1turn17search2

## Feed governance and Arla soy requirements

Arla’s current sourcing framework is **not a soy-free policy** and it is **not an import-free feed policy**. Arla’s published soy position says soy is used in feed for cows and that Arla’s historic ambition has been that soy fed to Arla milk producers is grown according to RTRS principles or equivalent, with RTRS certificates used to cover volumes not otherwise certified. The 2024 sourcing policy and action plan move the framing toward **deforestation- and conversion-free** soy, traceability, low-risk-country sourcing and externally verified DCF criteria, while still stating that RTRS credits are used for volumes with unknown deforestation/conversion risk. citeturn36search0turn36search2turn36search3

Arla’s wider sourcing page states a commitment to secure **DCF supply chains for soy, palm and forest fibre by 2025**. Its 2025 annual report then says the **share of indirect DCF soy rose to 82% in 2025 from 48% the previous year**, and its abridged annual report says **82% of soy used as feed at farm level was DCF in 2025**. The annual report also says soy volumes in feed had fallen and that Arla rewarded farmers for **reducing soy use or sourcing DCF soy** through FarmAhead. That is a real governance shift, but it is still not “soy-free”. citeturn36search7turn36search1turn36search4

Arla also explicitly notes that imported soy can carry a higher carbon footprint and encourages more home-grown feed where possible, but I did **not** find a reviewed Arla primary document saying Arla feed is now “import-free”. citeturn36search9turn36search1

## Manure to biogas and digestate use

Energistyrelsen’s biogas page says Denmark has **around 150 biogas plants** and that manure is the primary input. The same official page states that in **2021–2022**, slurry and other manure made up **just under 75% of biomass input at agricultural plants**. It also states that using manure for biogas reduces greenhouse-gas emissions from livestock and makes nutrients in the manure more plant-available. Danish energy statistics further show that **biogas production reached 31.7 PJ in 2023**, with around **82% of the produced biogas upgraded and injected into the gas grid** that year. citeturn29search0turn32search2turn33search6turn33search0

On digestate, the reviewed Danish fertiliser regulation treats **afgasset biomasse** as a recognised fertiliser stream inside the nutrient-accounting system. The 2025/26 fertiliser order requires monthly nutrient sampling when digestate is marketed, and it includes digestate in farm nutrient ledgers and storage rules. In other words, digestate use as fertiliser is not informal; it is explicitly regulated as part of the fertiliser/nutrient management regime. citeturn34search2turn35view4turn26view0

What I did **not** recover from the reviewed primary-source set was a clean, current national figure for the **share of all Danish manure sent to biogas** or a single official national tonnage for digestate applied back to land. Older Energistyrelsen studies discuss lower historical shares, but they are not suitable as a current benchmark figure for this request. That is therefore marked as **needs-data**, not estimated. citeturn32search13turn32search9

### Short judgement

For a circular-Nordic benchmark, Denmark currently presents a **very large, highly externalised livestock system** with strong manure-management and nutrient-accounting regulation, a mature manure-to-biogas infrastructure, and a policy stack that is moving from generic regulation toward a more spatially differentiated **land, nitrogen and GHG transition architecture**. But the most important caution is this: the reviewed primary texts support saying that **major restructuring is politically agreed and partly being implemented**, not that the full Green Tripartite package is already complete and fully enacted in law. On swine specifically, the latest official statistics reviewed do **not** document a presently enforced nationwide pig downscaling. citeturn39view1turn39view2turn24view0turn22view1turn22view3

### Do not say list

Do **not** say Denmark is a Norway pilot.

Do **not** say a general livestock CO2e tax is already in force now, unless that is re-checked against post-June-2026 enacted law.

Do **not** say Denmark has already legally ordered a nationwide pig-herd reduction.

Do **not** say Arla is soy-free or import-free.

Do **not** convert L&F dairy export revenue into an “export share of milk output” without a published conversion method.

Do **not** treat Green Tripartite agreement text as identical to enacted statute. citeturn22view1turn23view6turn36search0turn36search2

### Transferability note

What Nordic systems can plausibly learn from Denmark is the **institutional coupling** of manure, nutrient accounting, crop norms, spatial targeting, and energy recovery. The Danish case also shows how a high-export livestock system can be pushed toward circularity through **measured nutrient balances, land conversion funds, and manure-to-biogas integration**, rather than through a single blunt herd cap. citeturn25search1turn22view4turn29search0turn32search2

What is **not directly transferable** is the structural baseline: Denmark’s dairy and pig sectors are much more export-oriented and much more processing-integrated than Norway’s, and Denmark’s policy design is tied to its own geography of coastal nitrogen loads, its large piglet-export model, and its deep biogas build-out. So the benchmark is useful for **instrument design and systems integration**, but not as a simple blueprint for herd structure, trade exposure, or land-climate constraints elsewhere in the Nordics. citeturn39view1turn39view3turn24view0turn33search6
